newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW-India Thermax pushes into water purifiers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-India Thermax pushes into water purifiers.

text.p: Indian energy and environment management group Thermax plans to grab a chunk of the nation's huge water purifier market when it launches a range of ozonisers early next month, company officials said.

Thermax joined hands with American water treatment giant Culligan Water Technologies Inc in May to set up Thermax Culligan Ltd, a 50-50 joint venture to manufacture and market an entire range of water purifier products in India.
"The first launch of ozonisers is round the corner," Thermax managing director Abhay Nalawade told Reuters in a recent interview at his headquarters in the western city of Pune.
"We have a variety of products which will be launched progressively starting from July-August this year, going up to next July or August," he added.
Nalawade said the Indian market for water purifiers was potentially huge, and he expected purifier sales to bring in one billion rupees ($28 million) annually by 2000.
The size of the Indian market for water purification systems is roughly 2.5 billion rupees at present, industry sources estimate, and it is expected to grow to 10 billion by 2000.
Thermax's potential competitors include Videocon Appliance Ltd, Usha Shriram and Singer, which are all working out strategies to enter the sector.
"The demand is huge, so it's a question of tapping it well. Roughly we are estimating we should do about one billion rupees' business in three years' time," Nalawade said.
"Presently drinking water is offered in only one form -- predominantly the mineral water bottle," Nalawade added. "For 14 rupees a bottle, it's very expensive and not even reliable."
The Thermax product range will enable consumers to choose a technology that matches their specific purification needs.

"Right now the two significant players are based on the ultraviolet light and ion-exchange processes," Nalawade said. "We're entering with reverse osmosis, ultrafiltration, ozonisers, and a host of other options."
Thermax, whose core business is boilers, heat recovery systems, chemicals and pollution control equipment, did not see water purifiers as consumer durables, Nalawade said.

"We think water is not like a consumer durable," Nalawade said. "A fridge is a fridge is a fridge, whereas water treatment products differ from water to water. In coastal areas, for instance, reverse osmosis will be the appropriate treatment method, but in northeastern areas it'll be ion removers."
He added: "In most places there will be bacteria and virus trouble for which ozonisers are appropriate, and in some few city places ultrafiltration would do."
Nalwade said Thermax's marketing strategy envisioned three types of consumer needs for water.

"We're talking of three types of water, water at home, water in travel and water at work," he said. "Options differ for the way that water is dispensed. So the third segment is five-gallon water bottles with dispensers.
"For water in transit, we're talking of vending machines at railway stations and cinema halls. So we'll make very reliable and safe water in all the places in the most economical form."
Few of Thermax's sales would fit the usual consumer durable pattern, Nalawade said.

"For example, if we sell a water treatment scheme to Coke or Pepsi, individually it would look like a consumer durable sale, but for us it would be thousands of machines at a time, so it would be more like an institutional, or industrial, sale."
